docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Team 107 is building a Simple Educational Robotic Arm: a low-cost desktop arm that performs a repeatable pick-and-place sequence and is meant for students, educators and hobbyists who are learning robotics and embedded systems. The system is split into three boards, each built around its own PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano and owned by one team member. The Arm Motion Control board drives the arm joint's 6 V gearmotor through a FAN8100N H-bridge and reports when the arm is in position. The Gripper & Object Handling board opens and closes a servo gripper and senses grip force with an FSR 402. The User Controls & Safety board reads the emergency stop, start/pause button and speed knob, and shows the system state with LEDs and a buzzer. The boards share eight signals over a daisy-chained 8-pin ribbon cable (SAFE_OK, RUN_REQ, GRIP_CMD, OBJ_HELD, ARM_IN_POS, SPEED_SET, GRIP_FORCE and GND), so each board can be built, tested and replaced on its own while the safety signal from the User board can stop all motion at any time.

docs.title: Team Charter
docs.text: Our team is committed to designing and building a robotic arm system mock up (temporary) that actually works. We value clear communication, shared accountability, and treating this project as more than just an assignment: it's a chance to build real engineering skills and something worth putting in our portfolios. We agree to show up prepared, communicate honestly when something isn't working, and support each other so that every member leaves this project having learned something real and having contributed meaningfully to the final result.

docs.title: Product Mission Statement
docs.text: Our mission is to design a low-cost, modular desktop robotic arm system mock up that enables to achieve precise, repeatable automated pick-and-place tasks at a much lower barrier to entry, freeing up human effort for higher-value work.

docs.title: User Needs and Benchmarking
docs.text: Project goal: Our team is developing a low-cost, modular desktop robotic arm mock-up capable of performing precise, repeatable automated pick-and-place tasks. The purpose of the project is to demonstrate how repetitive manual work can be automated while keeping the system accessible to students, makers, and beginning robotics users. The design should prioritize: 1.) Precise and repeatable movement 2.) Reliable pick-and-place operation 3.) Low cost 4.) Easy setup and calibration 5.) Simple programming and control 6.) Modular hardware and software 7.) Safe operation 8.) Educational value Target User: The primary users identified for this project are: 1.) Engineering students learning robotics, embedded systems, controls, and programming. 2.) STEM educators who need a hands-on robotics demonstration or laboratory platform. 3.) Hobbyists and makers who want an inexpensive platform for experimentation. 4.) Beginning robotics programmers who need an approachable system for learning. 5.) Small-scale automation users who want to demonstrate simple repetitive automation.

docs.text:
The ranked needs were carried into the Product Requirements (PR-01 to PR-18) and into the three-board design shown on the Team Block Diagram:

Need category (rank) Where it appears in the current design Safety (1) User Controls & Safety board: normally closed E-stop drives SAFE_OK on the ribbon; every board stops when SAFE_OK is 0 or the cable is unplugged Accuracy & Repeatability (2) Arm Motion Control board: regulated 6 V motor rail and PWM speed control, so the same command gives the same motion every cycle Gripper & Object Handling (3) Gripper & Object Handling board: servo claw with an FSR 402 force sensor; the arm waits for OBJ_HELD before carrying the object Programming & Control (4) One simple state machine per board on the PIC18F57Q43, with speed set from a knob (Software Proposal) Power, Stability & Physical Design (5) Low-voltage 9 V adapters with fuses and reverse-polarity protection; separate motor and logic rails Calibration, Maintenance & Repair (6) Socketed parts, Curiosity Nanos on headers and screw terminals, so parts can be replaced without desoldering Cost & Accessibility (7) Common through-hole parts; three subsystem BOMs total about $255 Sensors, Vision & Expansion (8) Spare-pin expansion headers on each board for later sensors; vision is left for future work Documentation & Troubleshooting (9) Test points, status and debug LEDs, and the team and individual websites Education & User Experience (10) Simple start, pause, stop and speed controls with clear LED and buzzer feedback Assembly, Wiring & Components (11) Keyed 8-pin ribbon cable with one signal per wire (Message Structure)

docs.title: Project Objective
docs.text:
Our project aims to develop a low-cost, modular desktop robotic arm capable of performing precise and repeatable automated pick-and-place tasks. The system is intended to demonstrate how repetitive tasks can be automated while remaining accessible to engineering students, STEM educators, hobbyists, makers, and beginning robotics programmers. The product requirements were developed from the user needs identified during the Voice of the Customer benchmarking process. Existing products such as the Elephant Robotics myCobot 280, Yahboom DOFBOT, DOBOT Magician, Hiwonder xArm 1S, and Adeept 5-DOF Robotic Arm Kit were examined to identify desirable features and common problems. The primary objectives of the product are to:

  1. Provide precise and repeatable robotic movement.
  2. Reliably grasp, move, and release objects.
  3. Maintain a low overall system cost.
  4. Make assembly and calibration straightforward.
  5. Provide simple and understandable programming and control.
  6. Use modular hardware and software that can be expanded.
  7. Provide clear documentation and troubleshooting information.
  8. Provide an educational platform for learning robotics and embedded systems.
  9. Operate safely in a classroom, laboratory, or desktop environment.
  10. Provide a stable physical platform for repeated pick-and-place operations.

The final design should balance performance, affordability, accessibility, and educational value rather than focusing exclusively on maximum industrial performance.

docs.title: Target group
docs.text: Engineering Students Students are expected to be one of the primary users of the robotic arm. The system should allow students to learn about robotics, embedded systems, programming, sensors, motors, control systems, and automation through hands-on experimentation. STEM Educators Teachers and instructors may use the robotic arm as a classroom demonstration or laboratory platform. The system should therefore be easy to set up, demonstrate, and explain. Hobbyists and Makers Hobbyists should be able to use the robotic arm for experimentation, custom programming, and small automation projects without requiring expensive industrial equipment. Beginning Robotics Programmers The system should provide a relatively low learning curve so that users with limited robotics experience can begin programming and operating the arm. Small-Scale Automation Users The system should demonstrate basic automation concepts such as repetitive movement, object sorting, and pick-and-place operations.

docs.title: Secondary Stakeholders
docs.text: Project Team The engineering team is responsible for designing, assembling, programming, testing, and documenting the product. Future Designers and Developers Because the system is intended to be modular, future users should be able to modify or expand the hardware and software without redesigning the entire system. Manufacturers and Suppliers Manufacturing stakeholders need components that are affordable, available, compatible, and practical to assemble.

docs.title: Use Case #1: Engineering Student Performing Pick-and-Place
docs.text: An engineering student uses the robotic arm in a laboratory to learn about automated pick-and-place operations. The student places several small objects within the designated workspace and starts the robotic arm. The arm moves to a predefined position, activates the gripper, picks up an object, moves to another predefined position, releases the object, and returns to its starting position. The student then modifies the program to change the object's starting or ending position. User Requirements The system should: Complete the pick-and-place sequence consistently. Position the gripper accurately enough to grasp the intended object. Repeat the sequence multiple times without requiring manual recalibration. Allow the user to modify movement parameters. Provide understandable programming examples. Allow the student to observe the relationship between software commands and physical movement. Provide a safe method of stopping the arm if unexpected movement occurs. Verification This use case can be verified through a repeated pick-and-place test. The arm will be commanded to perform the same operation multiple times and the success rate, positioning error, and calibration stability will be recorded.

docs.title: Use Case #2: STEM Educator Demonstrating Robotic Automation
docs.text: A STEM educator uses the robotic arm during a classroom demonstration. The educator demonstrates how a repetitive manual task can be automated by programming the arm to move objects between two locations. Students observe the movement and then modify the program to change the movement sequence. User Requirements The system should: .Be simple enough to demonstrate without extensive setup. .Provide clear startup instructions. .Provide clear programming examples. .Allow students to modify the robotic sequence. .Operate safely around users. .Provide visible or understandable feedback about the system's operating state. .Be sufficiently reliable to complete a classroom demonstration without repeated troubleshooting. Verification The educator setup procedure will be timed and documented. The system will also be tested through repeated demonstrations to determine whether the arm can complete the programmed task consistently.

docs.title: 1. Hardware / Product Design
docs.text: The robotic arm should use a compact desktop form factor suitable for a laboratory, classroom, or workbench. The mechanical design should prioritize: 1.1 Stable operation. 1.2 Repeatable joint movement. 1.3 Reliable object handling. 1.4 Accessible components. 1.5 Modular construction. 1.6 Easy maintenance. 1.7 Low vibration. 1.8 Compact size. 1.9 Affordable components. 1.10 The arm should include an end effector capable of securely gripping the intended demonstration objects. 1.11 The mechanical structure should be sufficiently rigid that repeated movement does not cause excessive movement or instability. Hardware Requirements The base shall remain stable during normal operation. The joints shall provide controlled movement. The gripper shall securely hold the intended test objects. Components should be replaceable individually when practical. Wiring should be organized and protected from moving components. The system should provide an accessible emergency stop or software-controlled stop mechanism.

docs.title: 2. Software / Functionality
docs.text: The software should provide simple control of the robotic arm while allowing advanced users to modify the system. The system should support: 2.1 Manual movement. 2.2 Programmed movement. 2.3 Pick-and-place sequences. 2.4 Position control. 2.5 Gripper control. 2.6 Calibration. 2.7 Basic error handling. 2.8 Future sensor integration. 2.9 Future computer-vision integration. 2.10 The software should use a modular structure so that additional functions can be added without completely rewriting the control system. Software Requirements The software will: Allow the user to command individual robotic movements. Allow the user to execute a programmed sequence. Allow the user to control the gripper. Provide a method for calibration. Provide clear instructions for starting the system. Provide understandable examples for beginning programmers. *Allow future sensors or accessories to be integrated.

docs.title: 3. Interactivity & User Experience
docs.text: The robotic arm should provide an approachable user experience for users with limited robotics experience. The user interface should prioritize: 3.1 Simple controls. 3.2 Clear feedback. 3.3 Understandable error messages. 3.4 Straightforward calibration. 3.5 Accessible documentation. 3.6 Minimal unnecessary setup. 3.7 The system should allow a beginner to progress from basic manual movement to programmed automation. 3.8 The user should not need extensive robotics knowledge to perform the basic pick-and-place demonstration.

docs.title: 4. Customization
docs.text: The system should be designed so that users can modify or expand the robotic arm. Potential customization should include: 4.1 Different end effectors. 4.2 Additional sensors. 4.3 Computer vision. 4.4 Alternative control interfaces. 4.5 Different programmed movement sequences. 4.6 Additional objects or sorting tasks. 4.7 Software modifications. 4.8 Future robotic arm improvements. 4.9 The modular design should allow components to be replaced or upgraded without requiring replacement of the complete system.

docs.title: 5. Manufacturing
docs.text: The product should use commonly available components where practical to reduce cost and simplify replacement. Manufacturing considerations include: 5.1 Low component cost. 5.2 Availability of replacement components. 5.3 Repeatable assembly. 5.4 Accessible fasteners and connectors. 5.5 Organized wiring. 5.6 Modular components. 5.7 Minimal specialized manufacturing equipment. 5.8 Assembly instructions should be clear enough that a user with basic technical skills can construct or service the system.

docs.title: 6. Regulations
docs.text: 6.1 The product shall use a low-voltage power system suitable for a desktop educational environment and shall properly insulate exposed electrical connections. 6.2 The robotic arm shall incorporate mechanical or software-based joint limits to prevent movement beyond the safe operating range of each joint. 6.3 The product shall include an accessible emergency stop or power-disconnect mechanism capable of immediately stopping robotic motion. 6.4 The base shall remain stable without tipping or significant displacement when the robotic arm operates at its maximum specified payload and reach. 6.5 The end effector shall securely grasp and release objects within the specified payload range without damaging the objects during normal operation. 6.6 The product shall complete at least 100 consecutive pick-and-place cycles without mechanical failure or loss of basic functionality. 6.7 The robotic arm shall include protection against motor overload or prolonged stalled conditions to reduce the risk of overheating and component damage. 6.8 The product shall provide documentation specifying safe operating procedures, maximum payload, workspace limitations, assembly, and calibration requirements.

docs.title: Step 1: Introduction and Overview
docs.text:
The goal of this project is to develop a low-cost desktop robotic arm capable of performing precise and repeatable automated pick-and-place tasks. The system is intended to provide an accessible platform for engineering students, STEM educators, hobbyists, makers, and beginning robotics programmers to learn and experiment with robotics, embedded systems, programming, and automation.

The purpose of this design ideation process is to explore a wide range of possible features and design solutions that can satisfy the user needs and product requirements identified in the previous stages of the project. These ideas will be organized, evaluated, and combined into three distinct robotic arm design concepts.

docs.title: Step 3: Organizing and Ranking Generated Ideas
docs.text:
After generating possible features for the robotic arm, the ideas were reviewed and organized into groups based on the function they perform. Similar ideas were placed together so that the team could compare different solutions to the same design problem.

The ideas were evaluated primarily according to the highest-priority user needs identified during the User Needs and Benchmarking stage. These included accuracy, repeatability, reliable pick-and-place operation, affordability, ease of use, programmability, stability, and safety.

A three-level ranking system was used:

  • High Priority — Directly supports the primary function or a critical user need.
  • Medium Priority — Improves usability, flexibility, or performance but is not required for the basic system.
  • Low Priority — Useful for future development but adds complexity or is not necessary for the initial prototype.

docs.title: Step 4: Product Concepts
docs.text:
After organizing and ranking the generated ideas, the highest-priority features were combined into three distinct robotic-arm concepts. Each concept addresses the project's primary goal of creating a low-cost desktop robotic arm capable of precise and repeatable pick-and-place operations. However, each concept emphasizes a different approach to meeting the user needs.

The three concepts are:

  1. Concept 1 — Simple Educational Robotic Arm
  2. Concept 2 — Modular and Expandable Robotic Arm
  3. Concept 3 — Precision Automated Robotic Arm

docs.title: Concept 1: Simple Educational Robotic Arm
docs.text:
The first concept focuses on simplicity, affordability, and ease of use. This design is intended primarily for students and beginning robotics users. It minimizes unnecessary components while still providing the functions required to demonstrate automated pick-and-place operation.

The arm would use servo motors to control a rotating base, shoulder, elbow, and gripper. A two-finger gripper with rubber grip pads would provide a simple method for picking up lightweight objects.

The system would be controlled by a microcontroller and connected to a computer through USB. Users could manually control the joints during setup and then create stored movement sequences for automatic operation.

The second concept focuses on modularity, customization, and future expansion. This design would allow students and hobbyists to modify the robotic arm for different experiments without replacing the entire system.

The arm would use modular mechanical sections and standardized electrical connectors. A quick-change end-effector mounting system would allow the standard gripper to be replaced with other tools.

Expansion connections would also be included for sensors and future accessories. A camera mounting location could allow computer-vision experiments to be added later.

The third concept focuses on accuracy, repeatability, and automated operation. This design places greater emphasis on reliable repetitive pick-and-place performance.

Position feedback would be incorporated into the joints to help determine the actual position of the arm. Homing switches would establish a repeatable reference position when the system starts.

The software would support coordinated joint movement, adjustable speed, stored positions, and repeating automated movement sequences. Object detection or grip confirmation could also be incorporated to verify that an object was successfully picked up before continuing the sequence.

docs.title: How the decision was made
docs.text:
The team compared the three concepts against the product requirements and against what three students can build, wire and program in one semester with a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano on each board. Each concept was discussed against four questions:

  1. Does it meet the core requirements? All three concepts can run a programmed pick-and-place sequence (PR-01) and stop safely (PR-12).
  2. Can it stay inside the budget and the class rules? These are PR-17 and PR-14: through-hole parts, no breakout modules without approval, parts in stock and inside their ratings.
  3. Is it approachable for a beginner? This covers PR-15 and PR-16.
  4. Can the work be split so that every member owns a board with its own sensor or actuator? This is required by the course.

Concept 1 (Simple Educational) was selected as the base design. It has the lowest cost and complexity and the strongest beginner focus, which matches the project's mission of a low barrier to entry. Concept 3 (Precision) was set aside for the first prototype: joint feedback on every axis, homing switches and coordinated multi-joint control would need more sensors, more firmware and more calibration than the schedule allows. From Concept 2 (Modular), the team kept the modular electrical architecture: separate boards, standard connectors and spare I/O for future sensors. Concept 2's mechanical tool changer and camera mount were not kept.

The selected design is therefore Concept 1 with Concept 2's modular board structure:

docs.title: How the final design differs from the concepts
docs.text:
The final design deviates from the ideation in three places:

  • No joint position feedback or homing switches in the first prototype. Concept 3's joint feedback, and the potentiometer in an early Arm board design, were removed to keep the prototype simple and within budget. The arm runs the joint motor at a set speed for a set time and then reports ARM_IN_POS. To keep this upgrade path open (PR-11), the Arm board brings out an analog-capable pin and 3.3 V on its expansion header, so a potentiometer or magnetic encoder can be added later without a new PCB.
  • One DC-motor joint instead of three servo joints. The three-board split needs each board to use a different peripheral: H-bridge PWM, servo PWM with an ADC, and user I/O. A DC gearmotor with an H-bridge on the Arm board meets this, and it is enough to demonstrate a repeatable pick-and-place motion.
  • Boards talk over eight parallel signals, not a serial protocol. Early ideas included PC and serial command interfaces. The team chose an 8-pin ribbon with one wire per signal because it can be checked with a multimeter or LED, needs no protocol code to bring up, and keeps the safety signal independent of firmware. See Message Structure.

The updated design is shown in the Team Block Diagram.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This block diagram shows how our team's three boards work together in a pick-and-place robotic arm system. Each board uses a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano and handles one function: Arm Motion Control drives a 6 V gearmotor through a FAN8100N H-bridge; Gripper & Object Handling drives the Kitronik Klaw Mk2 servo and reads an FSR 402 force sensor; User Controls & Safety reads the E-stop, start/pause button and speed knob and drives the status LEDs and buzzer.

The boards are connected in a daisy chain with 8-pin ribbon cables. Pins 1–5 carry digital signals (SAFE_OK, RUN_REQ, GRIP_CMD, OBJ_HELD, ARM_IN_POS), pins 6–7 carry analog signals (SPEED_SET, GRIP_FORCE), and pin 8 is GND. Every sensor and actuator connects only to its own board's microcontroller, so only high-level status and command signals cross between boards. Arrows show signal direction.

Power is drawn the same way on every board: supply wiring is shown only from each source (9 V wall adapter or the PC's USB port) to its regulators, and the rail each block runs from is written in bold inside the block instead of drawing a supply line to it. Every Curiosity Nano runs at its factory 3.3 V from USB, so all ribbon signals are 0 / 3.3 V, and all grounds are common through ribbon pin 8.

docs.title: Research Question
docs.text:
• With only have 8-pin connectors. How to divide functionality across the team in a way that minimizes interconnections between teammates?
  • Does the system layout ensure each teammate meets minimum project requirements?
  • What are the risks to the current system if lose a teammate? How to de-risk the system design by grouping and/or distributing similar functions between teammates?

docs.title: Images
docs.text: Figure 1: Team block diagram (click the image to enlarge).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
1. Interconnections are kept to a minimum. The system is divided by physical ownership. Every sensor and actuator is wired only to the microcontroller on its own board, so no raw sensor or motor signal crosses a ribbon cable. Only high-level status and command signals are shared between boards: five digital, two analog and ground. This fits the whole team on one 8-pin connector, with one wire per signal.
  2. Every teammate meets the minimum project requirements. Each board has its own microcontroller, at least one ribbon connector, and at least one sensor or actuator, and each board uses different peripherals:
    • The Arm board has a DC gearmotor, an H-bridge and two PWM outputs.
    • The Gripper board has a servo (PWM) and a force sensor (ADC).
    • The User board has an E-stop, buttons, a speed knob (ADC), a DAC output for SPEED_SET, LEDs and a buzzer.
  3. Losing a teammate's board is a known risk.
    • If the User board is missing, SAFE_OK is never driven, so the system stays safely stopped and cannot run.
    • If the Gripper board is missing, the chain between the other two boards breaks, because it sits in the middle.
    • If the Arm board is missing, there is no motion.

We reduce these risks in four ways: (1) Every board's digital inputs have pull-down resistors and every board has test points or headers, so jumpers can simulate a missing teammate's signals and the other boards can still be tested. (2) The Gripper board passes pins 1–8 straight through from Connector 1 to Connector 2, so a single cable can run directly from the Arm board to the User board and the chain still works without the Gripper board. (3) All three boards use the same MCU, the same pin map and the same signal definitions, so any teammate can write a stub for another board's interface. (4) Safety does not depend on firmware messages. SAFE_OK is a dedicated wire from the User board's E-stop logic, and the pull-downs on the receiving boards turn a broken or unplugged cable into "stop".

docs.title: Design Decision-Making Process
docs.text:
Why three boards split by function. The arm was divided into Arm Motion Control, Gripper & Object Handling, and User Controls & Safety, so that each member owns one physical function end to end and each board can be built and tested alone. Grouping all user inputs and status outputs on one board puts the safety logic in a single place. Keeping the motor on its own board keeps motor current and noise away from the other boards.

Why an 8-pin parallel ribbon instead of a serial bus. Each signal has its own wire and exactly one driver, so the link needs no protocol firmware. It can be checked with a multimeter or an LED, and a fault on one wire does not corrupt the others. The two analog signals (SPEED_SET and GRIP_FORCE) are sent as voltages from a DAC, which avoids encoding numbers. Every Curiosity Nano runs at 3.3 V, so all ribbon signals use the same 0 / 3.3 V levels.

Why a daisy chain (Arm – Gripper – User). The Gripper sits in the middle because it exchanges signals with both other boards, and it passes the ribbon through 1:1 so the Arm and User boards still see every signal.

Why each board has its own power. Each board has its own 9 V adapter input and regulators for its actuator: the 6 V motor rail on the Arm board, the 5 V servo rail on the Gripper board and the 5 V buzzer rail on the User board. Every Nano is powered from USB. This way each board can be powered and tested alone, and motor current never flows through a teammate's board. Grounds are joined through ribbon pin 8.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The software controls the movement, positioning and gripping of the Simple Educational Robotic Arm. Each of the three boards (Arm Motion Control, Gripper & Object Handling, User Controls & Safety) runs its own firmware on a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The firmware is written in C with MPLAB X, XC8 and MCC Melody.

The three programs never send messages to each other. Each one reads and drives the eight parallel signals of the team ribbon cable, where every signal has one wire and one driver. A pick-and-place cycle is a handshake on those wires. The flowchart of one cycle is on the Process Diagram page, and the signal definitions and timing are on the Message Structure page.

docs.title: Software Objectives
docs.text:
The proposed software will:

  1. Initialize each board's peripherals with every output low and the motor and servo stopped, so the system powers up safe.
  2. Let the user start, pause and stop the sequence and set the arm speed from the User board.
  3. Drive the arm joint between a pick position and a place position, with speed set by PWM.
  4. Close the gripper until the FSR 402 shows enough force, then report that the object is held.
  5. Sequence the arm and gripper through the ARM_IN_POS → GRIP_CMD → OBJ_HELD handshake.
  6. Stop all motion whenever SAFE_OK goes low (E-stop pressed, fault, or cable unplugged) and show the state with LEDs and the buzzer.

docs.title: Firmware Structure (all three boards)
docs.text:
Every board uses the same simple structure, so any teammate can read or stub another board's code:

  • MCC-generated drivers: clock (HFINTOSC 64 MHz), pins, ADC, PWM, DAC and UART, depending on the board.
  • One main loop with a state machine: INIT → IDLE → RUN states… → STOP. The loop runs every 1 ms from a timer tick.
  • Safety check at the top of every loop: if SAFE_OK = 0, the board goes to STOP before doing anything else.
  • Debug output: a debug LED and an optional printf over the Nano's virtual COM port (UART). This UART goes to the PC only, not to the other boards.

docs.title: Proposed Software Operating Sequence
docs.text: Figure 1: One pick-and-place cycle across the three boards (also on the Process Diagram page; click to enlarge).

docs.title: Step 1: System Initialization
docs.text:
Each Curiosity Nano runs SYSTEM_Initialize().

  • Motor PWM and servo outputs start stopped.
  • All ribbon outputs start low.
  • The Arm board's H-bridge inputs are also held low by pull-down resistors during reset.

docs.title: Step 2: Wait for Safe and Run
docs.text: The Arm board waits until SAFE_OK = 1 and RUN_REQ = 1. Both come from the User board: the E-stop is released and the Start/Pause button has been pressed. While waiting, the User board blinks the green LED.

docs.title: Step 3: Safety Check (every loop)
docs.text:
On all three boards, SAFE_OK = 0 forces the STOP state:

  • the Arm board sets both PWM outputs to 0 %;
  • the Gripper board holds its position;
  • the User board turns on the red LED and sounds the buzzer.

After SAFE_OK returns, the user must press Start again; the boards do not resume on their own.

docs.title: Step 4: Arm Movement to Pick
docs.text: The Arm board reads SPEED_SET with its ADC and drives the joint toward the pick position with forward PWM. The joint runs at the set duty cycle for the programmed move time, then the board stops the motor and sets ARM_IN_POS = 1 and GRIP_CMD = 1.

docs.title: Step 5: Gripper Operation
docs.text: When the Gripper board sees GRIP_CMD = 1, it sends servo pulses to close the Kitronik Klaw Mk2.

docs.title: Step 6: Force Sensor Measurement
docs.text: The FSR 402 signal is buffered by the MCP6004 and read by the Gripper board's ADC. The board also outputs the force as a voltage on GRIP_FORCE, from its DAC, so the User board can display it.

docs.title: Step 7: Gripper Control
docs.text:
• Force reaches the threshold: the Gripper board stops closing and sets OBJ_HELD = 1.
  • No grip within the time limit: the gripper opens. The Arm board then clears GRIP_CMD and retries once; if the retry also fails, it signals a fault on its debug LED.

docs.title: Step 8: Move to Place and Release
docs.text:
When the Arm board sees OBJ_HELD = 1:

  1. It clears ARM_IN_POS and drives the joint to the place position with reverse PWM.
  2. It sets ARM_IN_POS = 1 and GRIP_CMD = 0.
  3. The gripper opens and clears OBJ_HELD.

docs.title: Step 9: Repeat
docs.text: The User board counts completed cycles from ARM_IN_POS and OBJ_HELD. While RUN_REQ stays high, the cycle repeats. Pressing Start/Pause again clears RUN_REQ and the arm stops at the end of its current move.

docs.text:
The boards communicate over the 8-pin ribbon cable with one signal per wire, at 0 / 3.3 V logic. The two analog signals are 0–3.3 V voltages. There is no serial protocol between boards: a signal's level is the message. The full table of signals, drivers, meanings and timing is on the Message Structure page.

docs.title: Software Design Decision-Making
docs.text:
Why each board runs its own simple state machine. Each teammate can write, test and debug their firmware alone, with jumpers standing in for the other boards. A state machine with named states (IDLE, MOVE_TO_PICK, WAIT_GRIP, MOVE_TO_PLACE, RELEASE, STOP) maps one-to-one onto the process diagram, so the code is easy for a beginner to follow (PR-15, PR-16).

Why parallel signals instead of messages. The team first considered UART messages such as MOVE and GRIP_OPEN between boards. They were replaced with the 8-pin parallel signals for three reasons:

  • no parsing, framing or checksum code is needed, and each board's link code is a few pin reads and writes;
  • every signal can be checked with an LED or a meter during bring-up (PR-18);
  • a crashed board or broken cable shows up as a 0 on its wires, which the receivers already treat as "stop" (PR-12).

Why the safety check comes first in every loop. Stopping does not wait for the current move to finish or for a message to arrive. SAFE_OK is a hardware level that every board reads at least once a millisecond.

Why the arm uses timed moves for now. The first prototype has no joint position sensor. The Arm firmware keeps the move time and duty cycle as named constants, so they are easy to tune. A future encoder or potentiometer on the Arm board's expansion header can replace the timer without changing the rest of the state machine (PR-11).

docs.title: Research Question
docs.text:
How do three independent microcontrollers, linked only by eight parallel wires, take turns to complete a pick-and-place cycle safely, and what happens when something goes wrong?

The diagram answers this by showing, for every step, which board acts, which signal it changes, and which board is waiting for that change. It also shows the stop path that every board checks on every loop.

docs.title: Process Diagram
docs.text: Figure 1: Process diagram for one pick-and-place cycle (click to enlarge).

docs.title: How to Read the Diagram
docs.text:
1. Power-up. Each board initializes with every output low and its motor or servo stopped. The Arm and Gripper boards wait.
  2. Start. When the E-stop is released, the User board sets SAFE_OK = 1. When the user presses Start, it sets RUN_REQ = 1 and outputs the speed knob value on SPEED_SET.
  3. Move to pick. The Arm board drives the joint forward with PWM on RC4 at the requested speed. When the move is done it sets ARM_IN_POS = 1 and GRIP_CMD = 1.
  4. Grip. The Gripper board closes the claw until the FSR 402 reaches the force threshold, then sets OBJ_HELD = 1. It also outputs the measured force on GRIP_FORCE, and the User board displays it.
  5. Move to place. The Arm board clears ARM_IN_POS and drives the joint in reverse with PWM on RC5. At the place position it sets ARM_IN_POS = 1 and GRIP_CMD = 0.
  6. Release. The gripper opens and clears OBJ_HELD. The User board counts the cycle. If RUN_REQ is still 1, the cycle repeats.
  7. Stop path (any time). If SAFE_OK becomes 0 because the E-stop is pressed, a fault occurs, or the cable is unplugged, the Arm board sets both PWM outputs to 0 %, the Gripper board holds, and the User board turns on the red LED and buzzer. The user must release the E-stop and press Start again to continue.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
1. We divided the system by physical ownership. Every sensor and actuator is wired only to the microcontroller on its own board, so no raw sensor or motor signal crosses the ribbon cable. Only status, command and two 0–3.3 V analog values are shared, and they fit in 7 signal pins plus ground.
  2. Each board meets the subsystem requirements. Each board has its own microcontroller, a ribbon connector, and at least one sensor or actuator:
    • the Arm board has the DC gearmotor and FAN8100N H-bridge;
    • the Gripper board has the servo claw and the FSR 402 force sensor;
    • the User board has the E-stop, Start/Pause button, speed knob, LEDs and buzzer.

  3. What happens if one board is missing, and how we reduce the risk.

    • Losing the User board: SAFE_OK is never driven, the pull-downs read 0, and the system stays safely stopped.
    • Losing the Arm board: no motion happens.
    • Losing the Gripper board: GRIP_CMD has no answer, so the Arm board times out and stops.

    We reduce these risks in four ways:

    1. Every input has a pull-down, so a missing board or cable reads as "stop".
    2. Each signal has one driver, so any board can be tested alone by pulling its inputs high or low with jumpers.
    3. All three boards use the same PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano and the same ribbon pin order, so any teammate can write a stub for another board.
    4. The Gripper board passes every ribbon pin straight through (1:1), so the User board's SAFE_OK reaches the Arm board on the same wire.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Team 107's boards do not exchange serial messages. Each "message" is the level of one wire on the 8-pin ribbon cable that links the User Controls & Safety, Gripper & Object Handling and Arm Motion Control boards in a daisy chain. This page defines every signal and the order in which they change during a cycle. The Process Diagram shows the same cycle from each board's point of view.

docs.title: Signal Definitions
docs.text:
All logic signals use 0 / 3.3 V levels, because all three Curiosity Nanos run at 3.3 V. Each signal has exactly one driver. The Gripper board passes all eight pins straight through (1:1), so every board sees every signal.

Pin Signal Type Driver Receiver(s) 1 / high means 0 / low means Unplugged reads 1 SAFE_OK Digital User (RD0) Arm, Gripper Safe to run Stop now 0 (stop) 2 RUN_REQ Digital User (RD1) Arm Start / continue cycle Pause after current move 0 3 GRIP_CMD Digital Arm (RD2) Gripper Close gripper Open gripper 0 (open) 4 OBJ_HELD Digital Gripper (RD3) Arm, User Object held (force ≥ threshold) Not holding 0 5 ARM_IN_POS Digital Arm (RD4) Gripper, User Arm is at its target Arm is moving 0 6 SPEED_SET Analog 0–3.3 V User DAC (RA2) Arm ADC (RA1) Higher voltage = faster 0 V = slowest 0 V 7 GRIP_FORCE Analog 0–3.3 V Gripper DAC (RA2) User ADC (RA1) Higher voltage = more force 0 V = no force 0 V 8 GND Ground — all Common reference

Electrical rules

  • Every digital input has a 10 kΩ pull-down, so a missing cable or an unpowered board reads 0.
  • Every digital output has a 330 Ω series resistor, which limits current if two boards ever drive the same wire by mistake.
  • Analog inputs have a 1 kΩ / 0.1 µF RC filter before the ADC.
  • The connectors are keyed 2 × 4 shrouded headers, so the cable cannot be plugged in backwards.

docs.title: Message Sequence
docs.text: Figure 1: Signal sequence for one pick-and-place cycle and the stop path (click to enlarge).

docs.title: Handshake Rules
docs.text:
1. Nothing moves without SAFE_OK = 1. Both the Arm and Gripper boards check SAFE_OK at the top of every loop. A 0 stops all motion immediately, whatever state the board is in.
  2. The Arm board leads the cycle. It starts only when SAFE_OK = 1 and RUN_REQ = 1, and it is the only board that drives GRIP_CMD and ARM_IN_POS.
  3. The Gripper board acts only when the arm is in position. It closes on GRIP_CMD = 1 only while ARM_IN_POS = 1, and opens on GRIP_CMD = 0.
  4. The Arm board waits for OBJ_HELD before carrying an object. If OBJ_HELD does not rise within the grip timeout, the arm clears GRIP_CMD and retries once, then shows a fault.
  5. Restart is deliberate. After any stop, the User board drops RUN_REQ. The user must release the E-stop and press Start again.
  6. Analog values are advisory. SPEED_SET only scales the arm's PWM duty, and GRIP_FORCE is only displayed. A bad analog value cannot start motion on its own.
